title: AgroSense ARIA
lede: An offline-capable AI farming platform: a self-healing LoRa mesh of ESP32-S3 sensor nodes on a custom 4-layer PCB, reporting to a Raspberry Pi hub that runs seven on-device ML models and a three-tier LLM assistant — with no internet connection required.

meta.Stack: ESP32-S3 · LoRa · Raspberry Pi · Edge AI

hero.alt: The ARIA dashboard running on the Raspberry Pi hub
hero.caption: ARIA dashboard, live

p: ARIA is my M.Tech final-year project: an AI farming platform that works without an internet connection. A LoRa mesh of ESP32-S3 sensor nodes reports to a Raspberry Pi hub, and everything — sensing, inference, irrigation decisions, and the assistant a farmer talks to — happens on hardware sitting in the field.
The nodes run on the AgroSense board line I designed alongside it. Revision 3 is the current hardware.

Nodes take one of three roles — root hub, sub-hub or leaf — and the network scales from 2 to 100 of them. A leaf can be promoted to a sub-hub when the topology needs it, so losing one node doesn't split the network.

Airtime is divided by TDMA scheduling so a hundred nodes on one frequency don't collide, with an RTC-driven time-sync cascade keeping their slots aligned. I wrote about 7,260 lines of ESP32-S3 firmware for this, AES-128 on the link, with the nodes deep-sleeping between scheduled readings — that's what takes battery life into years.

Seven models on the Raspberry Pi, all offline: disease detection, irrigation scheduling, fertiliser planning, yield prediction, crop recommendation, anomaly detection over the sensor stream, and an ensemble that reconciles them into one plan.
The farmer-facing assistant is a three-tier cascade — cloud when there's signal, a local model when there isn't — with speech in and out in English, Hindi and Telugu.

Irrigation automation sits behind a four-level autonomy controller, from advisory through to acting on its own. Every action is logged and any automated one has a 60-second undo. Irrigation mistakes are expensive and slow to reverse.

specs: Claude Haiku 4.5 → Claude Code CLI → Ollama qwen2.5:0.5b
Vosk STT, Edge-TTS — EN / HI / TE

metrics.s: all inference runs on the farm

title: AgroSense Node rev 3
lede: The current AgroSense node: four copper layers, solar MPPT with a selectable panel input, a matched LoRa front end, and three independently switched supply rails.

hero.alt: 3D render of the AgroSense revision 3 board, top side
hero.caption: Revision 3 — top side

p: The AgroSense node went through three revisions: rev 1 was a 2-layer prototype, rev 2 moved to four copper layers, and rev 3 is the one in the field. Each build folded in what the previous one's bring-up found rather than patching faults on the bench.
Rev 3 is a four-layer mixed-signal board and the hardware ARIA runs on.

A LoRa radio with a matched RF feed and a U.FL launch, so the antenna can be chosen for the site without respinning the board. The antenna keepout and the stitched ground around the feed stay clear of the switching and digital regions — that continuous reference plane is the reason for going to four layers.

Power is solar MPPT charging with a jumper-selectable panel voltage, Li-ion charge and protection, and USB-C in. The 3.3 V, 5 V and 12 V rails are independently enabled, so idle sensors can be switched off between readings instead of sitting biased.

microSD logging, an IMU and I²S audio, RGB status indicators, a smaller board outline and broken-out I²C and GPIO headers for field expansion. Gerbers, BOM and netlists went out after a DRC and DFM review on each run.
The gallery below has all four copper layers and both 3D renders.

specs: LoRa SX1262, matched feed to U.FL

title: AgroSense Node rev 2
lede: The revision that went to four copper layers — MPPT solar harvesting and a multi-rail power tree on 82 × 80 mm, and the bring-up that found two real layout mistakes.

hero.alt: AgroSense 2.0 four-layer board, 3D render of the top side
hero.caption: AgroSense 2.0 — top side

p: The AgroSense node went through three revisions: rev 1 was a 2-layer prototype, rev 2 moved to four copper layers, and rev 3 is the one in the field. Each build folded in what the previous one's bring-up found rather than patching faults on the bench.
Rev 2 is where the board went to four copper layers — 82 × 80 mm, 195 components.

Solar input through an MPPT charge controller with a wide input range, so the same board works behind panels of quite different sizes. Battery charging and reverse-current protection are handled separately from the harvesting stage, with a load switch between the pack and the rails downstream.

A buck gives the 3.3 V logic rail; boost converters give 5 V and a selectable 9/12 V for sensors that need more. Keeping those separate rather than sharing one supply is what makes it possible to shut most of the board down between readings.
Two faults on the first assembled boards, both mine, both layout rather than part choice.

The USB data pair to the UART bridge was routed reversed, so the board wouldn't enumerate. And the boost converter section didn't route cleanly — the ground return and via placement around the switching node weren't good enough.
Both went into rev 3 rather than getting patched on the bench. That's the honest version of this board: it worked, with two defects that taught me more than the parts that came out right first time.

title: AgroSense Node rev 1
lede: The two-layer prototype that started the AgroSense line — scheduled soil and climate sampling, RTC-driven deep sleep, solar charging and a long-range uplink to a gateway.

hero.alt: AgroSense 1.0 node block diagram showing sensing, power and radio sections
hero.caption: System block diagram

p: The AgroSense node went through three revisions: rev 1 was a 2-layer prototype, rev 2 moved to four copper layers, and rev 3 is the one in the field. Each build folded in what the previous one's bring-up found rather than patching faults on the bench.
Rev 1 is the two-layer prototype — the one that had to prove the idea held together before spending four layers on it.

Measure soil moisture, water level, temperature and humidity at set intervals and send them to a gateway, instead of someone walking the field with a meter. Controller, radio, real-time clock, solar charging and the wired sensor interface all on one board.

It was built around being asleep most of the time: an RTC wakes the controller on schedule and the board drops back into deep sleep between readings. That's the difference between a node that lasts a season and one that needs a visit every fortnight.
The two-layer layout worked but left no room to improve the radio's reference plane, and the power tree was tighter than it wanted to be. Both fed straight into rev 2.

title: Dletabotix Kit Hardware
lede: Two boards behind a classroom robotics kit: a multi-function controller that students assemble themselves, and a USB-host programmer that lets a whole bench of BBC micro:bits be reflashed without a PC.

hero.alt: Dletabotix kit hardware — artwork not published
hero.caption: Artwork not published

p: At Dletabotix I design the electronics for their classroom robotics kits. Two boards so far, both cost-optimised 2-layer designs, because a classroom set is bought by the dozen.

The constraint that shapes both is that the user is actively trying to get it wrong, and is meant to. Every external connection is keyed so a sensor can't be seated backwards, the through-hole parts are the ones students solder, and the microcontroller sits in a socket so a board killed by a wiring mistake is a swap rather than a rework job.

An Arduino Nano carrier with dual H-bridge drivers across four motor channels, keyed connectors for ultrasonic, IR, light and RGB modules, and Bluetooth for control from a phone. Power is a two-cell Li-ion charger with protection, fed from USB-C or a barrel jack, with switching regulators for the rails. A robot on a bench with a cable in it should still drive, so charge and load current are managed separately.
A micro:bit is normally programmed by dragging a file onto the USB drive its debug interface exposes — fine with one, miserable with thirty and one teacher.

This board uses an ESP32-S3 in USB host mode to mount that drive itself and write the firmware image, sourced over Wi-Fi or from on-board storage. Load it once, then plug in each micro:bit in turn. A TFT and buttons drive the flow, and a firmware-enabled 5 V rail means the target is only live when the programmer intends it.
First-article checks on each board — power rails, peripherals, current draw — then signal-level fault-finding with a scope and logic analyser across prototype iterations.

On the firmware side I also wrote the kit's mode handling. The line sensors calibrate themselves on every run rather than trusting a trimmer set at the factory, which is what lets the kit work on whatever the classroom floor happens to be.

specs: Microcontroller module on a carrier socket
Keyed connectors — ultrasonic, IR, light, RGB
BBC micro:bit, via its USB mass-storage interface
Firmware-enabled 5 V to the connected board
Over Wi-Fi or from on-board storage

title: Grid OS Telematics & Audio
lede: The boards behind Grid OS's vehicle trackers and cellular audio devices — 2- and 4-layer designs in Altium, and the production panels they ship on.

hero.alt: Close-up of a densely populated radio front end — shielded IC, crystals and matching network
hero.caption: Radio front end

p: During my time at Grid OS I worked on the boards behind their vehicle trackers and their cellular audio devices — the countertop and handheld units that read a payment out loud.

Both are built around a cellular module with a SIM interface, battery-backed power and an antenna that has to work inside someone else's enclosure. I did schematic capture and layout on 2- and 4-layer stackups in Altium: impedance-controlled routing for the USB and radio traces, antenna keepouts and ground fencing, the audio codec section, and the switching supplies that feed all of it.

I also drew the production panels these boards ship on — V-score separation, breakaway rails, fiducials and tooling holes, laid out to suit the assembler's machine rather than just to fit. Three of them are in the gallery below.
Each design went out as a manufacturing package rather than a board file: Gerbers, drill files, test-point mapping, an impedance profile and a BOM, after design-rule and manufacturability checks.

specs: Antenna keepouts, ground fencing, impedance control
Panelisation, Gerbers, drill, test points, BOM

title: 32-bit ALU — RTL to GDSII
lede: A complete open-source ASIC flow for a 32-bit arithmetic logic unit: 29 operations, a Brent–Kung parallel prefix adder, 7,372 standard cells placed and 8,135 nets routed with zero DRC violations on 0.18 µm.

meta.Programme: NIELIT Centre of Excellence in Chip Design

hero.alt: Detail of the ALU standard-cell layout in Magic, showing routed metal over cell rows
hero.caption: Magic layout detail

p: A 32-bit ALU taken all the way from Verilog to a fabrication-ready GDSII during an internship at NIELIT's Centre of Excellence in Chip Design — using only open-source tools: Yosys, GrayWolf, Qrouter and Magic.
It does 29 operations: signed and unsigned add, subtract, multiply and divide, all sixteen boolean functions, and three shift types.

Arithmetic speed comes from a Brent–Kung parallel prefix adder, which trades wiring for a carry path that grows logarithmically rather than linearly. It ends up being the critical path of the whole design.

Multiply and divide run as sequential state machines over 32 cycles instead of combinational arrays — a deliberate area-for-latency trade, since a full 32-bit combinational multiplier would have dominated the cell count for operations that aren't on the hot path.
7,372 standard cells, a 5.24 ns critical path for about 190 MHz, and 8,135 nets routed with zero DRC violations on 0.18 µm. Verification passed 66 of 66 randomised tests across three seeds.
Mostly it's an argument that the open-source flow is mature enough for real digital blocks, not just teaching examples.

title: Arduino Nano — 12 V Input
lede: A pin-compatible Arduino Nano rebuilt for industrial supplies: 12 V input through a switching pre-regulator, USB-C with ESD protection on the data lines, and debug headers actually brought out.

hero.alt: 3D render of the custom Arduino Nano board, top side
hero.caption: 3D render, top

p: A stock Arduino Nano regulates its input with a linear regulator. Feed it 12 V — which is what an industrial or automotive supply gives you — and the regulator burns the difference as heat, which limits what the rest of the board can draw before it shuts down.
I kept the Nano pinout so existing shields and code still work, and replaced the front end.
A buck converter takes 12 V to 5 V, and an LDO derives 3.3 V from that, so the analogue rail isn't carrying switching ripple directly.

USB-C instead of mini-B, with ESD protection on the data lines — that's the failure mode that actually kills development boards on a busy bench. Beyond the standard headers I brought out separate UART, I²C and ICSP, which sounds minor until you're trying to get a logic analyser onto a bus buried under a shield.

specs: Nano pinout, plus UART, I²C and ICSP

title: Network Rover + Surveillance
lede: A Wi-Fi controlled rover carrying live video, a pan-tilt camera and a robotic arm, with cloud telemetry and an eight-channel relay board for home automation — the project that pulled everything from four years together.

hero.alt: Network controlled rover with robotic arm and camera mast
hero.caption: Completed rover

p: My B.Tech final-year project: three things in one build — a drivable rover with live video, a remotely operated robotic arm, and a home automation controller, all reachable over the network from one interface.

A Raspberry Pi runs the Python side — camera streaming, cloud communication, command parsing. Arduino boards handle the real-time work: motors, servo timing, sensor polling. That split is what keeps the video from stuttering every time a motor changes direction.

The camera sits on a two-axis mount driven through an I²C servo controller, which keeps sixteen servo channels off the Pi's timing-sensitive GPIO. Ultrasonic and IR sensors handle obstacles; fire and temperature sensors cover the surveillance side.
Telemetry goes to a cloud service for logging and remote commands, and appliance switching is exposed through Google Assistant as well as the dashboard.
A Li-ion pack with a BMS feeding a step-down converter. The rover runs motors, servos, a Pi and a camera at once, and the Pi is the first thing to brown out when the supply sags as the motors start.

specs: Li-ion pack with BMS, XL4015E step-down

title: Night Vision Rover
lede: A Raspberry Pi rover driven from a Python program over the network, with an infrared camera on a two-axis servo mount for low-light surveillance.

hero.alt: Night vision rover chassis with infrared camera mounted on servos
hero.caption: Rover with camera mast

p: A Raspberry Pi rover driven over the network from a Python program on a PC — drive commands, camera angle and lighting all across the same link. The infrared camera is the point: it works in the dark.
Camera orientation is two servos, horizontal and vertical, commanded through an I²C controller so the Pi isn't bit-banging servo pulses while also streaming video.

Commands arrive over Wi-Fi, get parsed, and dispatch to separate modules for motion, lighting and camera angle. Keeping those apart rather than in one loop is what made it maintainable enough to keep extending.
The camera mount and the command-parsing approach both carried straight into the final-year rover.

title: Bluetooth Multi-Task Rover
lede: One chassis, three behaviours — manual drive from an Android app, line following, and obstacle avoidance — with mode and message display on an onboard LCD.

hero.alt: Bluetooth multi-task rover on a workbench with LCD and sensor array
hero.caption: Assembled rover

p: The rover takes single-character commands over Bluetooth from an Android app and switches between three modes: manual drive, line following on infrared sensors, and obstacle avoidance on ultrasonic ranging.
A 16×2 LCD shows the current mode, live sensor state, or whatever text you send it from the phone — which turned out to be the feature everyone actually wanted to play with.
Arduino C++ on an Uno, motors through a dual H-bridge. The mode switch is a state machine so transitions are clean rather than leaving a motor latched from the previous mode.
One function per behaviour over shared drive primitives — which is what made it easy to bolt a vacuum mechanism onto the same codebase for the cleaning robot.

title: Bluetooth Home Automation
lede: Relay-switched mains appliances driven from an Android app over Bluetooth, with a scene mode that sequences several devices from a single command.

hero.alt: Bluetooth home automation build with relay modules wired to appliances
hero.caption: Relay control build

p: Lights, fans and other mains appliances switched by relays from an Arduino, driven from an Android app over Bluetooth. Each command maps to a device and an action, and a scene mode sequences several devices from one command — for shutting a room down without sending five separate instructions.

Anything switching mains deserves respect. The relay modules are opto-isolated from the logic side, the low-voltage and mains sections are physically separated, and it runs off a properly regulated supply rather than a bench adapter.
The firmware tracks relay state rather than inferring it, so what's on is always known.

title: Vacuum Cleaning Robot
lede: An autonomous cleaner on a custom acrylic chassis — centrifugal suction, a PWM-controlled sweep brush, ultrasonic collision avoidance and an infrared cliff sensor.

hero.alt: Autonomous vacuum cleaning robot on a custom acrylic chassis
hero.caption: Completed robot

p: A cleaning robot on a chassis I cut from acrylic — dual DC motors through an H-bridge, a centrifugal fan for suction, and a PWM-controlled sweep brush pulling debris into the intake. Bluetooth starts and stops it, and a physical toggle arms the cleaning mechanism separately from the drive so you can move it without it running.
Collision avoidance is ultrasonic. Cliff detection — the part that stops it driving off a step — is an infrared sensor pointed at the floor, which is the cheap and reliable way to solve that.
Status streams over serial, which matters more than it sounds: watching the sensor values live is the only practical way to tune the thresholds for a particular floor.

title: Colophon
lede: How this site is built: hand-written HTML, CSS and JavaScript, no framework, no build step, and a theme switch modelled on a PCB layer stackup.

p: The site is modelled on a printed circuit board, because that's what I do. The hero is a routed board with traces at 45° and 90°, carrying signal pulses along the copper. Section headers are silkscreen legends, project cards carry component designators, and the theme switch is a layer selector: silkscreen, copper, or bare FR-4 substrate.
The previous version was an adapted Bootstrap template. This one is written from scratch.
No framework, no bundler, no package manager — one stylesheet, one script and static HTML, so deploying is a git push and nothing can rot in a dependency tree.

The old version loaded nine vendor libraries totalling about 22 MB, most of them unused on every page. All of it is gone. The lightbox is a native <dialog>, the filter is nine lines of JavaScript, and the typing effect is a setTimeout.

Every image is pre-generated to AVIF and WebP at four widths and served through <picture>. The original library was 114 MB of unoptimised JPEG and PNG; the derivatives are a fraction of that, and any single page pulls only a handful. Fonts are self-hosted variable subsets — three families, 100 KB.

Scroll reveals use CSS scroll timelines where the browser supports them, with an IntersectionObserver fallback. Navigating to a case study uses cross-document View Transitions so the card morphs into the page hero instead of flashing white.
All of it is gated on prefers-reduced-motion in both CSS and JavaScript. If you have reduced motion enabled, nothing here moves.

The previous version of this portfolio was adapted from R-TharunReddy/My_Portfolio under its original licence. None of that code remains, but the site ran on it for a long time and the credit is owed.
